analysis.one_liner: Limits mandatory overtime for nurses at Medicare-funded facilities to 12 hours a day and protects nurses who refuse.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 18 Senate cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote in the Finance Committee, dying when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred Medicare-participating hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and similar facilities from forcing nurses to work beyond their scheduled shift, more than 12 hours in a 24-hour period, or more than 80 hours in 14 days — except during a declared emergency. It would have protected nurses from retaliation for refusing forced overtime or reporting violations, let nurses file complaints with the Health and Human Services Department, and imposed fines of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with repeat offenders facing steeper penalties and public listing on an HHS website. It also directed HHS to study safe maximum work hours for nurses and OMB to check federal facilities' own overtime practices.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses at Medicare-participating facilities gain the right to refuse forced overtime beyond a 12-hour day or 80-hour two-week cap, backed by anti-retaliation protections, a federal complaint process, and fines on violating providers. Patients gain too: the bill's findings cite studies showing nurses working shifts of 12.5 hours or more were three times more likely to make errors, so limiting forced overtime is framed as a patient-safety measure. Nurses who want extra hours could still volunteer for them.

how_it_helps.text: Caps mandatory overtime: a provider could not require a nurse to work beyond the scheduled shift, more than 12 hours in any 24-hour period, or more than 80 hours in a consecutive 14-day period, with an exception only during a declared emergency — and the exception explicitly excludes labor disputes and consistent understaffing, so chronic short-staffing could not be used to justify forced overtime.

Protects nurses from retaliation: providers could not discharge, discipline, or discriminate against a nurse for refusing mandatory overtime, reporting violations to regulators or accreditors, cooperating in investigations, or discussing violations with coworkers, and could not report a nurse to a state disciplinary board for refusing forced overtime.

Gives nurses real enforcement tools: they could file complaints with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, providers would have to post notices of nurses' rights and publish schedules, knowing violations would carry civil money penalties of up to $10,000 each (harsher for repeat offenders), and penalized providers would be named publicly on HHS's website.

Aimed the limits at patient safety: the findings cite a 2004 Health Affairs study that nurses on shifts of 12.5 hours or more were three times as likely to commit an error, and a 2007 study linking nurse overtime to ICU infections, and cite an Institute of Medicine recommendation to cap work at 12 hours per 24 and 60 per week except in emergencies.

Directed follow-up studies: HHS would study and recommend safe maximum-hour standards for nurses, and the Office of Management and Budget would report within six months on whether federally operated facilities like VA and military hospitals had overtime practices inconsistent with the new rules.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, critical access hospitals, home health agencies, ambulatory surgical centers, rehabilitation agencies, rural clinics, and federally qualified health centers that bill Medicare would bear the cost: they could no longer fill staffing gaps by mandating overtime, so they would need to hire and retain more nurses, pay for more voluntary overtime, or run short in non-emergencies. Taxpayers would fund the HHS and OMB studies and the federal complaint and enforcement machinery. Some added staffing costs could eventually show up in healthcare prices.

drawbacks.text: The limits cover only mandatory overtime. A nurse could still voluntarily work far past 12 hours, and the bill's own findings note nurses reported being 'coerced' into overtime on hundreds of shifts — so fatigue-related risk would persist wherever nurses feel pressure to say yes.

Hospitals already struggling to recruit nurses would have to cover staffing gaps through hiring or volunteers, a real cost in a labor market the bill itself describes as short roughly hundreds of thousands of practicing nurses; smaller rural and critical access hospitals, which the bill also covers, would feel that squeeze hardest.

Enforcement would be complaint-driven and penalty-capped at $10,000 per knowing violation — small relative to hospital budgets — so deterrence would depend heavily on nurses knowing their rights and on HHS actually investigating and pursuing penalties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs to hospitals are real but the bill was designed to soften them: emergencies are carved out, voluntary overtime remains legal, and the forced-overtime ban gives facilities two weeks' worth of scheduling flexibility. Against that, the record the bill itself assembles — error rates tripling on long shifts, infections rising with overtime, nurses leaving the profession over forced hours — points to patient-safety and retention gains that likely outweigh the staffing expense. The main honest criticism is that a voluntary-overtime loophole and modest, complaint-driven enforcement could blunt the bill's effect in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Safe Nursing and Patient Care Act on July 20, 2007, joined by 13 original cosponsors including Hillary Clinton, Barack Obama, John Kerry, Chris Dodd, Barbara Mikulski, and Bernie Sanders.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over Medicare; that was the last action ever taken on it.

Eighteen senators cosponsored the bill in total — 16 Democrats, one Independent, and one Republican — but the Finance Committee never scheduled it for consideration and it never reached the Senate floor.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee with no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and other Medicare providers that use mandatory overtime to cover staffing gaps came out ahead — they never had to absorb the hiring costs or scheduling limits the bill would have imposed. Nurses working forced overtime and their patients got nothing.

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Fourteen additional senators
for.role: Cosponsors (16 Democrats and 1 Republican in total beyond Sanders)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, for 18 total.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: The Finance Committee, which he chaired, took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, and it was never reported to the floor.

against.name: Hospital industry
against.role: Hospitals and health systems relying on mandatory overtime staffing
against.what_they_did: Hospital groups have historically opposed federal caps on mandatory nurse overtime, arguing facilities need staffing flexibility during nursing shortages.

sides.party_line_note: All known support came from Democrats and one Independent, with a single Republican among the 18 cosponsors; since the bill never got a vote, no roll call shows where the broader Senate stood.

industries.note: Medicare-participating hospitals could no longer use mandatory overtime as a staffing model — no forced shifts past 12 hours a day or 80 hours in 14 days — and faced fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation plus public listing for penalties. They would have had to hire more nurses or rely on volunteers, raising staffing costs in exchange for fewer fatigue-related errors.

industries.industry: Home health agencies, clinics, and other covered Medicare providers
industries.note: The overtime limits and penalty regime extended beyond hospitals to home health agencies, ambulatory surgical centers, rural health clinics, rehabilitation agencies, and federally qualified health centers that bill Medicare.

industries.industry: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses
industries.note: Nurses would gain the legal right to refuse forced overtime beyond the caps, plus whistleblower-style protection from firing, discipline, or referral to state licensing boards, and a federal complaint channel.
